subject: Home Management
practicalPaper: Paper 3 is a 3-hour practical test for 100 marks conducted by a visiting examiner appointed by WAEC. Candidates carry out set household tasks such as planning and preparing meals, laundry and stain removal, sewing and repairs, cleaning and home care, and are marked on planning, procedure, hygiene and safety, and the quality of the finished work.

practicals.title: Identifying and removing common stains
practicals.aim: To identify common stains on household fabrics and remove them using suitable, safe stain-removal agents.
apparatus: Clean white cloths and old towels
materials: Stained cotton samples (blood, palm oil, ink, rust, tea, grass)
safety: Methylated spirit is flammable - use away from flames and in a ventilated room.
Wear gloves with bleach and never mix bleach with other chemicals.
Test any reagent on a hidden part of the garment first.
procedure: Identify the stain by colour, smell and feel, and classify it (protein, grease, tannin, dye, mineral).
Treat the stain while fresh: scrape off any solid deposit with a blunt knife.
Protein stains (blood, egg): soak in cold salt water (about 1 tablespoon salt in 500 ml cold water), then wash. Never use hot water first.
Grease (palm oil): place the stained area face down on a pad, dab from the back with methylated spirit or rub with detergent, then wash in hot water if the fabric allows.
Rust: cover with salt, squeeze lemon juice on it, leave in the sun, then rinse.
Tea or coffee: soak in warm borax solution, then wash.
Work from the outside of the stain towards the centre, rinse well and launder normally.
Record the stain, agent used and result in a table.
practicals.expectedObservations: Fresh stains come out more easily than old ones. Blood fades in cold salt water but sets if hot water is used first. Lemon and salt lighten rust in sunlight. Grease spreads unless treated from the back over an absorbent pad.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Borax solution: 15 g of borax in 500 ml warm water gives a concentration of 15/500 x 100 = 3% (mass/volume). Salt solution for blood: 15 g (1 tablespoon) salt in 500 ml cold water. Results table example: Blood / cold salt water / removed; Rust / lemon and salt / mostly removed; Palm oil / methylated spirit then detergent / removed after two treatments.
precautions: Treat stains as quickly as possible.
Use the mildest method first.
Work from the outside inwards to avoid a ring.
Rinse out all chemicals before laundering.
sourcesOfError: Old or set stains respond poorly.
Different fabrics react differently to the same agent.
commonMistakes: Using hot water on protein stains.
Rubbing hard and spreading the stain or damaging fibres.
Using bleach on coloured or woollen fabrics.
examTips: Classify stains and give the specific agent and method for each.
Always mention testing on a hidden area and rinsing afterwards.

checkQuestions.explanation: Hot water coagulates (sets) the protein; cold salt water loosens it.

checkQuestions.q: Which pair is used to remove rust stains?
checkQuestions.explanation: The acid in lemon with salt dissolves rust.

checkQuestions.q: Stains should be treated by working
options: from the outside towards the centre
checkQuestions.explanation: Working inwards prevents a spreading ring.

practicals.title: Laundering white and coloured cotton articles
practicals.aim: To sort, wash, rinse, dry and iron cotton articles using the correct laundry agents and processes.
safety: Check the care label before washing.
Unplug the iron after use and place it on its heel.
Never mix bleach with other chemicals.
procedure: Read care labels and sort articles: whites, light colours, dark colours; mend and remove stains first.
Test coloured fabrics for colour fastness by pressing a damp white cloth on a hidden seam.
Soak whites in detergent solution; wash in hot water, rubbing soiled parts (collars, cuffs).
Wash coloured articles separately in warm water, quickly, turned inside out.
Rinse thoroughly in several changes of water until no lather remains; add blue to the last rinse for whites if desired, and starch shirts.
Dry whites in the sun and coloured articles inside out in the shade.
Iron while slightly damp, at the setting for cotton, starting with double parts (collar, cuffs) then the large areas; air and fold.
practicals.expectedObservations: Clean whites look bright; coloured articles keep their colour when washed separately in warm water and dried in shade. Damp cotton irons smoothly.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Detergent dosage: the packet states 30 g per 4 litres of water. For a 10-litre bucket: 30/4 x 10 = 75 g. Using too much wastes detergent and needs more rinsing.
precautions: Do not leave coloured items soaking for long.
Rinse well to remove all detergent.
Use the correct iron temperature for the fabric.
sourcesOfError: Hard water reduces the effectiveness of soap.
commonMistakes: Washing whites and colours together.
Drying coloured items in strong sun.
Ironing over buttons and stains.
examTips: Name each stage in order: preparation, sorting, soaking, washing, rinsing, finishing (blue, starch), drying, ironing, airing.
Examiners award marks for testing colour fastness and reading labels.

checkQuestions.q: Why are coloured clothes dried inside out in the shade?

practicals.title: Laundering special garments: wool and silk
practicals.aim: To launder a woollen jumper and a silk scarf without shrinking, felting or damaging the fibres.
apparatus: Iron with low setting and pressing cloth
materials: Mild soap flakes or wool detergent
safety: Test water temperature with the elbow or a thermometer.
Keep the iron on a low setting for silk and wool.
procedure: Measure the jumper (length and chest) or draw its outline on paper before washing.
Prepare lukewarm water (about 30-40 °C) and dissolve mild soap completely.
Squeeze the garment gently in the suds - do not rub, twist or wring.
Rinse in several changes of water at the same temperature; add a little vinegar to the last rinse for silk to restore lustre.
Roll the garment in a towel to remove excess water.
Dry wool flat, pulled back to its original measurements, away from direct heat; hang silk in the shade.
Press silk on the wrong side with a cool iron while slightly damp; press wool under a damp pressing cloth if necessary.
practicals.expectedObservations: The jumper keeps its size and softness; the silk keeps its sheen. Rubbing or hot water would cause wool to felt and shrink.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Mixing water to the right temperature: 3 litres at 25 °C mixed with 1 litre at 80 °C gives (3 x 25 + 1 x 80) / 4 = 155 / 4 = 38.75 °C, within the 30-40 °C range for wool.
precautions: Keep the same temperature for washing and rinsing.
Never wring wool or silk.
Dry away from direct sunlight and heat.
sourcesOfError: Water cools during washing; temperature may fall below the target.
commonMistakes: Using hot water or strong detergent on wool.
Hanging a wet jumper so it stretches.
Ironing silk on a hot setting.
examTips: Give the reason for each step (e.g. "no rubbing - prevents felting").
Know the care-label symbols for hand wash and dry flat.

checkQuestions.q: Why should a woollen jumper be dried flat?
options: To prevent it stretching out of shape
checkQuestions.explanation: Heavy wet wool stretches if hung.

practicals.title: Simple garment repairs: darning, patching and sewing on buttons
practicals.aim: To repair worn and torn garments by darning a small hole, applying a patch and replacing a button.
safety: Keep pins in a pin cushion and count them in and out.
Carry scissors closed with the points down.
procedure: Darning: trim loose threads; on the right side, work rows of running stitches in one direction across the hole, extending 1-1.5 cm beyond it into firm fabric; then weave across these at right angles.
Patching: cut a patch on the same grain as the garment, larger than the worn area; turn under the edges, pin and tack on the right side.
Hem the patch neatly in place, turn to the wrong side, trim the worn area leaving turnings, and hem these down.
Button: mark the position; secure the thread; stitch through the holes over a pin to form a shank; wind the thread round the shank and fasten off on the wrong side.
Press each repair.
practicals.expectedObservations: A good darn is flat, even and blends with the fabric; a patch lies flat with matched grain; a button with a shank fastens easily without straining the fabric.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Patch size: hole 3 cm x 2 cm; allow 2 cm of firm fabric beyond the hole on every side plus 0.5 cm turning on every edge. Width = 3 + 2 x 2 + 2 x 0.5 = 8 cm; length = 2 + 2 x 2 + 2 x 0.5 = 7 cm. Cut the patch 8 cm x 7 cm.
precautions: Match thread colour, fibre and thickness.
Match the grain of the patch to the garment.
Do not pull darning stitches tight.
sourcesOfError: Inaccurate measurement of the worn area.
commonMistakes: Darning only over the hole and not into firm fabric.
Cutting the patch off-grain so it puckers.
Sewing a button flat without a shank on a thick coat.
examTips: Neat, even stitches, correct grain and pressing are the main marking points.
Give reasons for repairing early ("a stitch in time saves nine").

checkQuestions.q: Darning stitches should extend
options: about 1-1.5 cm into firm fabric around the hole
checkQuestions.explanation: Stitching into firm fabric anchors the darn.

checkQuestions.q: A hole 3 cm wide needs 2 cm margin and 0.5 cm turning each side. Patch width?
Why is a shank made when sewing on a button?
options: To allow room for the fabric of the buttonhole
checkQuestions.explanation: The shank lets the button sit on top of the buttonhole layer.

practicals.title: Sewing processes: seams, hems and neatening
practicals.aim: To work samples of a plain (open) seam, a French seam and a run-and-fell seam, and a turned-up hem.
materials: Cotton fabric pieces 20 cm x 15 cm
safety: Keep fingers away from the needle; switch off the machine when threading.
Do not sew over pins.
procedure: Plain seam: place right sides together, pin, tack and machine 1.5 cm from the edge; remove tacking, press open and neaten the edges (zigzag, overcast or pinking).
French seam: place wrong sides together, stitch 0.6 cm from the edge; trim to 3 mm; turn so right sides are together, press, and stitch 0.9 cm from the fold, enclosing the raw edges.
Run-and-fell seam: stitch a plain seam, trim one allowance to half, fold the wider one over it, press and machine or hem flat.
Hem: turn up 0.5 cm, then turn again to the hem depth, pin, tack and slip-hem or machine.
Press each sample and mount it on a labelled sheet.
practicals.expectedObservations: A French seam shows no raw edges and suits fine fabrics; a run-and-fell seam is flat and strong and suits shirts and work clothes; plain seams are flat and quick.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: French seam within a 1.5 cm allowance: first line 0.6 cm, trim to 0.3 cm, second line 0.9 cm from the fold. Check: 0.6 + 0.9 = 1.5 cm, so the finished seam line falls exactly on the 1.5 cm fitting line.
precautions: Stitch with an even seam allowance using the machine guide.
Press after each stage.
Tie off or back-stitch the ends of machine stitching.
sourcesOfError: Uneven seam allowance causes the finished width to vary.
commonMistakes: Starting a French seam with right sides together.
Not trimming enough, so threads poke through.
Puckering from wrong tension.
examTips: Label each sample and state where it is used.
Neatness, accuracy of measurement and pressing are marked.

checkQuestions.q: A French seam is started with
checkQuestions.explanation: Wrong sides together first, then right sides together to enclose edges.

checkQuestions.q: Which seam is best for a man's work shirt?
checkQuestions.explanation: It is flat and very strong.

checkQuestions.q: The standard seam allowance is usually
checkQuestions.explanation: 1.5 cm is the common seam allowance.

practicals.title: Using and caring for sewing equipment and tools
practicals.aim: To identify sewing tools, thread and use a sewing machine correctly and carry out simple machine care.
apparatus: Cutting shears, trimming scissors, pinking shears
safety: Switch off and unplug electric machines before threading or cleaning.
Keep shears closed when not in use.
procedure: Identify each tool and state its use.
Wind a bobbin, insert it in the bobbin case and thread the upper machine following the threading guide.
Raise the bobbin thread and stitch straight lines and curves on scrap fabric.
Check the stitch: adjust tension if loops appear on top or underneath.
Clean: remove the needle plate, brush out fluff, put one drop of oil at each oiling point, run the machine on scrap fabric to absorb excess oil.
Cover the machine and store tools in a sewing box.
practicals.expectedObservations: Correctly balanced tension gives stitches that look the same on both sides with the threads interlocking inside the fabric.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Stitch length check: on a 10 cm test line, count the stitches. If there are 40 stitches, stitch length = 10 cm / 40 = 0.25 cm (2.5 mm), a normal length for medium cotton.
precautions: Use the correct needle for the fabric.
Do not cut paper with fabric shears.
Oil sparingly.
sourcesOfError: Counting partial stitches at the ends of the line.
commonMistakes: Threading with the presser foot down, so tension discs are closed.
Pulling the fabric through the machine and bending the needle.
examTips: Know how to correct tension faults: loops underneath - tighten upper tension; loops on top - loosen upper tension.

practicals.title: Making household linen: a pillowcase
practicals.aim: To calculate the fabric needed for a housewife-style pillowcase and make it using suitable seams and hems.
safety: Handle shears carefully.
Switch off the iron after use.
procedure: Measure the pillow (width and length).
Calculate the fabric: width = pillow width + two seam allowances; length = twice the pillow length + flap + hem turnings.
Cut the fabric on the straight grain.
Hem one short end (narrow hem) and the other short end (deeper hem for the opening).
Fold to form the flap and the pillow pocket, right sides together, and stitch the side seams (or use French seams).
Turn right side out, press and fit on the pillow.
practicals.expectedObservations: The finished case fits the pillow snugly, the flap holds the pillow in place and the seams are neat inside.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Pillow 50 cm x 75 cm. Width = 50 + 2 x 1.5 = 53 cm. Length = 2 x 75 + 15 cm flap + 1 cm narrow hem + 4 cm deep hem = 170 cm. Cut one piece 53 cm x 170 cm.
precautions: Pre-wash cotton to allow for shrinkage.
Cut on the straight grain so the case hangs straight.
sourcesOfError: Pillows vary in size; measure each one.
commonMistakes: Forgetting seam allowances.
Cutting off-grain.
Leaving raw edges unneatened.
examTips: Show your calculation of fabric requirements.
Neat seams and pressing earn marks.

checkQuestions.explanation: Cotton may shrink in the first wash.

practicals.title: Identifying fibres by the burning test
practicals.aim: To identify cotton, wool/silk and synthetic fibres by how they burn, the smell given off and the residue left.
materials: Small yarn or fabric samples: cotton, wool, silk, polyester, nylon, polyester-cotton
safety: Work over a metal tray with water nearby.
Hold samples with tongs - melting synthetics drip and burn the skin.
Tie back hair and work in a ventilated room.
procedure: Cut small samples about 2 cm long.
Hold each sample with tongs and bring it slowly towards the flame; observe whether it shrinks or melts.
Put it in the flame and note how it burns.
Remove it and note whether it continues burning.
Note the smell (carefully waft towards the nose) and examine the residue when cool.
Record results in a table and identify each fibre.
practicals.expectedObservations: Cotton (cellulose) burns quickly with a yellow flame, smells like burning paper and leaves soft grey ash. Wool and silk (protein) burn slowly, curl away from the flame, smell of burning hair or feathers and leave a black crushable bead; they often stop burning away from the flame. Polyester and nylon melt and shrink from the flame, smell chemical and leave a hard bead that cannot be crushed.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Blend composition: a 200 g shirt labelled 65% polyester / 35% cotton contains 0.65 x 200 = 130 g polyester and 0.35 x 200 = 70 g cotton. Such a blend shows mixed results - it melts and leaves some ash and a hard bead.
precautions: Test small samples only.
Never test fabric while it is being worn.
sourcesOfError: Finishes and dyes can change burning behaviour.
Blends give mixed results.
commonMistakes: Confusing the soft ash of cotton with the crushable bead of wool.
Holding samples with fingers.
examTips: Record test, observation and inference in columns.
Group fibres as vegetable (cellulose), animal (protein) and synthetic.

practicals.title: Preparing and using local and commercial cleaning agents
practicals.aim: To prepare local cleaning agents (lemon and salt, wood ash, black soap) and compare them with commercial products for cleaning metal and other surfaces.
safety: Wood-ash water is alkaline and irritates skin - wear gloves.
Use abrasives gently on soft metals.
Keep polishes away from children.
procedure: Identify the agents: water, soaps and detergents, abrasives, polishes, acids, alkalis.
Lemon-salt paste: cut a lemon, dip in salt and rub tarnished brass; rinse and dry.
Wood-ash cleaner: soak sieved ash in water, strain, and use the liquid to scour greasy pots.
Use black soap solution on tiles and plastic surfaces.
Clean a second brass item with commercial polish following the instructions.
Compare the results, time and cost, and record in a table.
practicals.expectedObservations: Lemon and salt remove brass tarnish quickly; the cleaned metal is bright but must be dried well. Wood-ash water cuts grease. Commercial polish gives a longer-lasting shine.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Cost per cleaning session: commercial polish N2,400 for 200 ml, using 20 ml per session = 2,400/200 x 20 = N240. Local method: 2 limes at N100 each + salt N20 = N220. The local method is N20 cheaper per session.
precautions: Rinse off acids and alkalis completely.
Dry metals immediately to prevent water marks.
Test on a small area first.
sourcesOfError: Prices vary by market.
Degree of tarnish differs between items.
commonMistakes: Using coarse sand on lacquered or plated items.
Leaving lemon juice on metal so it marks.
examTips: Classify agents and give a local and a commercial example of each.
Give the surface each agent suits.

checkQuestions.q: Which local agent is best for removing tarnish on brass?
checkQuestions.explanation: The acid in lemon and the mild abrasive salt remove tarnish.

checkQuestions.q: Wood-ash water cleans grease because it is
checkQuestions.explanation: Ash contains alkaline potash that emulsifies grease.

practicals.title: Cleaning floors, surfaces and a functional area
practicals.aim: To clean a room (e.g. the sitting room or kitchen) systematically, caring correctly for tiled, terrazzo and wooden surfaces.
safety: Place a "wet floor" sign or warn others.
Do not stand on unstable chairs to reach high places.
Open windows for ventilation.
procedure: Ventilate the room and remove or stack movable items.
Work from top to bottom: remove cobwebs, dust high surfaces, then furniture.
Clean wooden furniture with a slightly damp cloth, dry, then polish along the grain.
Sweep the floor from the corners to the centre and collect the dust.
Mop tiled or terrazzo floors with detergent solution using the two-bucket method (wash and rinse), working towards the door.
Return furniture, empty buckets, wash and dry all cleaning equipment.
practicals.expectedObservations: Working top to bottom prevents re-soiling cleaned surfaces. The floor dries without streaks when rinsed and wrung well.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Room 4 m x 3.5 m: area = 14 m². One 5-litre bucket of detergent solution (25 ml detergent) covers about 10 m². Buckets needed = 14/10 = 1.4, so prepare 2 buckets (50 ml detergent in 10 litres).
precautions: Do not flood wooden floors with water.
Change dirty mop water often.
Use the right agent for each surface.
sourcesOfError: Coverage per bucket depends on how dirty the floor is.
commonMistakes: Sweeping before dusting high surfaces.
Mopping yourself into a corner.
Using abrasive powder on polished or formica surfaces.
examTips: State the order of work and the reason for it.
Name the material of each surface and its correct care.

checkQuestions.q: In cleaning a room, the correct order is to work
checkQuestions.explanation: Dust falls downwards, so start high.

checkQuestions.explanation: Polishing with the grain gives an even shine.

practicals.title: Making a bed with mitred (hospital) corners
practicals.aim: To make a bed neatly with mitred corners and calculate the size of sheet needed for a given mattress.
safety: Bend the knees and keep the back straight when lifting the mattress.
procedure: Strip the bed, air the mattress and turn it regularly.
Spread the bottom sheet right side up with the centre fold down the middle; tuck in at the head.
Make a mitred corner: lift the side edge to form a triangle, tuck the hanging part under the mattress, drop the triangle and tuck it in.
Tuck in the foot and the sides tightly so there are no wrinkles.
Add the top sheet (wrong side up), blanket and bedspread; turn down the top sheet over the blanket at the head.
Put on the pillowcases with the open ends away from the door and place the pillows.
practicals.expectedObservations: The bed is smooth and firm, the corners are neat 45° folds and the bedding does not come loose when sat on.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Mattress 135 cm x 190 cm x 20 cm deep, with 20 cm tuck-in on each side. Sheet width = 135 + 2 x 20 (depth) + 2 x 20 (tuck) = 215 cm. Sheet length = 190 + 2 x 20 + 2 x 20 = 270 cm.
precautions: Keep sheets centred.
Pull each layer taut before tucking.
sourcesOfError: Mattress depth varies; measure before buying sheets.
commonMistakes: Wrinkles in the bottom sheet.
Pillowcase openings facing the door.
Sheets too small to tuck in.
examTips: Describe each step in order; examiners look for airing and mitred corners.

Why should a mattress be aired and turned?
options: To keep it fresh and wear it evenly
checkQuestions.explanation: Airing removes moisture; turning spreads wear.

checkQuestions.q: Pillowcase openings should face
checkQuestions.explanation: Openings away from the door look neater.

practicals.title: Flower arrangement for the home
practicals.aim: To make a triangular (or crescent) flower arrangement applying the elements and principles of design.
materials: Fresh flowers (e.g. hibiscus, ixora, bougainvillea, zinnia)
safety: Cut stems away from the body.
Wash hands after handling plants with irritant sap.
procedure: Pick flowers early in the morning, cut stems at a slant and stand them in water.
Soak the foam and fix it firmly in the container.
Place the tallest stem to set the height (about 1½-2 times the container height), then the side stems to set the width.
Fill in with foliage and focal flowers, keeping the largest/brightest flowers low in the centre.
Check balance, proportion, rhythm and harmony of colour from the front.
Top up with water and place the arrangement where it suits the room.
practicals.expectedObservations: The finished arrangement has a clear outline, a focal point, and balanced colour and proportion with no foam showing.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Container height 20 cm. Tallest stem above the rim = 1.5 x 20 = 30 cm (up to 2 x 20 = 40 cm). Side stems are usually about two-thirds of the main stem: 2/3 x 30 = 20 cm.
precautions: Recut stems under water to prevent air locks.
Remove leaves that would sit below the water line.
Change water regularly.
sourcesOfError: Flowers wilt in heat, changing the shape.
commonMistakes: Stems all the same length.
Overcrowding.
A container that overpowers the flowers.
examTips: Name the principles of design used (balance, proportion, emphasis, rhythm, harmony).
State how to make arrangements last longer.

checkQuestions.q: For a 20 cm container, the tallest stem should be about
Why are stems cut at a slant?
options: To increase the area for taking up water
checkQuestions.explanation: A slanted cut exposes more surface for water uptake.

checkQuestions.q: The focal point of an arrangement is usually placed
checkQuestions.explanation: The focal point anchors the design near the centre.

practicals.title: Reading an electricity meter and calculating a bill
practicals.aim: To read a household electricity meter and calculate the energy used and the cost, including VAT.
materials: A sample electricity bill or tariff sheet
safety: Do not open or touch meter covers or wiring.
Read the meter from a safe distance.
procedure: Record the previous meter reading from the last bill (or read the meter at the start of the period).
Read the meter at the end of the period, reading from left to right.
Subtract the previous reading from the present reading to find units used (kWh).
Multiply by the tariff per kWh to find the energy charge.
Add VAT and any fixed charge to find the total bill.
Suggest ways the family can reduce the bill.
practicals.expectedObservations: The meter reading increases as electricity is used. Appliances with heating elements (iron, water heater, electric cooker) use the most energy.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Previous reading 12,450 kWh; present reading 12,735 kWh. Units used = 12,735 - 12,450 = 285 kWh. Energy charge at an illustrative tariff of N68 per kWh = 285 x 68 = N19,380. VAT at 7.5% = 0.075 x 19,380 = N1,453.50. Total = N20,833.50.
precautions: Read each digit carefully.
Check whether the tariff band applies to your area.
sourcesOfError: Misreading a dial meter where the pointer lies between two numbers.
Tariffs change - use the current figure.
commonMistakes: Subtracting the wrong way round.
Forgetting VAT.
examTips: Show the subtraction, the multiplication and the VAT step separately.
Give at least three ways to save electricity.

Which is a good way to reduce the electricity bill?
options: Leave lights on in empty rooms
Iron clothes in bulk at one time
checkQuestions.explanation: Ironing in bulk avoids reheating the iron many times.

practicals.title: Purifying water for household use
practicals.aim: To purify muddy water by settling, filtration, boiling and chlorination, and to store it safely.
apparatus: Clean covered storage container with a tap
materials: Clean sand and gravel for a filter
safety: Use bleach in the correct small dose only.
Do not drink water during the experiment.
procedure: Observe and record the appearance of the raw water.
Add a little alum, stir and leave to settle for several hours (sedimentation).
Pour off the clear water and filter it through a clean folded cloth or a sand filter.
Boil one portion at a rolling boil for at least 1 minute and allow to cool, covered.
Chlorinate another portion: add 2 drops of 5% bleach per litre of clear water, stir and wait 30 minutes.
Store purified water in a clean, covered container and draw it off with a tap or clean cup.
practicals.expectedObservations: Alum makes particles clump and settle, leaving clearer water. Filtration removes remaining particles. Boiling kills germs; chlorinated water has a faint chlorine smell after 30 minutes.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Chlorine dose: 2 drops per litre. For a 20-litre jerrycan = 2 x 20 = 40 drops. Using about 20 drops per ml, 40 drops = 2 ml of bleach.
precautions: Filter cloudy water before boiling or chlorinating.
Store in clean, covered containers.
Do not put hands or cups into stored water.
sourcesOfError: Drop size varies between droppers.
Very cloudy water needs a higher chlorine dose.
commonMistakes: Boiling for only a few seconds.
Storing purified water in dirty containers.
examTips: List methods in the right order: sedimentation, filtration, then disinfection (boiling or chlorination).
Name sources of water and their likely contamination.

practicals.title: Preparing a monthly family budget
practicals.aim: To prepare a family budget, calculate the percentage spent on each item and present it as a pie chart.
materials: Family income and expenditure details (real or given)
safety: Keep real family financial details private.
procedure: List all sources of income and find the total.
List fixed expenses (rent, school fees) and variable expenses (food, transport, utilities).
Allocate amounts, including savings, so that expenditure does not exceed income.
Calculate each item as a percentage of income and its pie-chart angle (percentage x 3.6°).
Draw and label the pie chart.
Review: identify where savings can be made.
practicals.expectedObservations: Food usually takes the largest share of a family budget; setting aside savings first helps the family meet emergencies.
precautions: Check that percentages add to 100% and angles to 360°.
Include savings and an allowance for emergencies.
sourcesOfError: Rounding of percentages and angles.
commonMistakes: Spending more than income.
Leaving out savings.
Drawing pie sectors without measuring angles.
examTips: State the steps in budgeting and the advantages of a budget.
Show working for each percentage.

practicals.title: Preparing and serving a family lunch
practicals.aim: To plan, prepare and serve a balanced lunch for a family of four, including table setting and service.
safety: Keep pan handles turned in.
Wash hands and use separate boards for raw meat.
Keep a fire blanket within reach when frying.
procedure: Plan a balanced menu (e.g. rice and stew with fish, sautéed vegetables, fruit salad, water).
Calculate quantities and write a market list and time plan.
Prepare and cook the dishes in the order of the time plan, cleaning as you work.
Set the table for four with suitable cutlery and a centrepiece.
Dish up attractively and serve hot food hot and cold food cold.
Clear the table, wash up and evaluate.
practicals.expectedObservations: Food is ready at the stated time, the menu contains all classes of food, and the table is neat and correctly set.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Raw rice allowance about 90 g per person: 4 x 90 = 360 g. Fish 1 piece (about 120 g) each: 4 x 120 = 480 g. Time plan works back from serving at 1:00 pm: rice takes 30 minutes, so start it by 12:25 pm to allow 5 minutes for dishing.
precautions: Taste and adjust seasoning before serving.
Cover food to keep it hot and clean.
sourcesOfError: Cooking times vary with stove heat.
commonMistakes: Unbalanced menu (e.g. rice with yam).
No time plan.
Untidy work area.
examTips: The visiting examiner awards marks for planning, hygiene, method, results and serving - plan each.
Write menus neatly in the correct order of courses.

options: Rice and stew with fish, vegetables and fruit
checkQuestions.explanation: It contains all the classes of food.

practicals.title: Home safety check and first aid practice
practicals.aim: To identify hazards in the home, check a first aid box and practise first aid for burns, cuts and nosebleeds.
safety: Practise only on uninjured volunteers.
Use gloves when dealing with blood.
procedure: Inspect the home or a model room for hazards: loose wires, slippery floors, chemicals within reach of children, open wells, kerosene stored near fire.
Check the first aid box against a list and replace missing items.
Burns: cool under running water for at least 20 minutes, cover loosely with cling film or a clean non-fluffy dressing.
Cuts: apply direct pressure with a clean pad, raise the injured part, then dress.
Nosebleed: sit the person leaning forward, pinch the soft part of the nose for 10 minutes, breathe through the mouth.
Record hazards found and suggest prevention.
practicals.expectedObservations: Most home accidents come from falls, burns, cuts, electric shocks and poisoning, and can be prevented by simple measures.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: First aid box check: 10 of 12 required items present = 10/12 x 100 = 83.3%. The two missing items must be replaced. Nosebleed pressure time = 10 minutes; burn cooling time = at least 20 minutes.
precautions: Never tilt the head backwards for a nosebleed.
Do not apply oil or toothpaste to burns.
Get medical help for serious injuries.
sourcesOfError: Checklists may not suit every home.
commonMistakes: Tilting the head back in a nosebleed.
Using unclean materials on wounds.
examTips: For each accident give cause, prevention and first aid.
List the contents of a first aid box with uses.

checkQuestions.q: For a nosebleed, the person should
options: lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose
checkQuestions.explanation: Leaning forward stops blood running down the throat.

Which helps prevent poisoning of children at home?
options: Keeping medicines and chemicals locked away and labelled
checkQuestions.explanation: Locked, labelled storage prevents accidental poisoning.

practicals.title: Market survey and comparing unit prices
practicals.aim: To carry out a market survey of selected household goods and use unit prices to identify the best buy.
materials: Price information from at least two markets or shops
safety: Go in groups with a teacher's permission and keep personal belongings safe.
procedure: Choose items to survey (rice, tomato paste, detergent, cooking oil) and prepare a survey form.
Visit at least two outlets and record brand, size and price for each item.
Calculate the unit price (price per kg, per g or per litre).
Compare and identify the best buy, also considering quality, storage and the family's needs.
Write a short report with recommendations.
practicals.expectedObservations: Larger packs and bulk purchases usually have a lower unit price, but are only economical if the family can store and use them before they spoil.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Tomato paste: 70 g sachet N250 -> 250/70 = N3.57 per g; 400 g tin N1,200 -> 1,200/400 = N3.00 per g; the tin is cheaper per gram. Rice: 50 kg bag N85,000 -> N1,700 per kg; retail N2,000 per kg. Saving = N300 per kg (15%), or N15,000 on 50 kg.
precautions: Compare the same quality and units.
Check expiry dates and packaging.
sourcesOfError: Prices change daily and between sellers.
Different brands differ in quality.
commonMistakes: Comparing total prices instead of unit prices.
Buying in bulk without storage space.
examTips: Define market survey and give its uses.
Show unit-price working for each comparison.
